title: Nations Across the Continent
bigQuestion: How did the land shape the many different ways Native peoples lived across North America?

story.title: Market Day Under the Great Mound
story.kicker: Around the year 1100, the biggest city north of Mexico stood beside the Mississippi River, a short walk from where St. Louis is today.
paragraphs: The sun comes up over the river, and the city is already awake. A girl named Little Fawn walks with her mother toward the great plaza. Smoke rises from hundreds of houses with thatched roofs. Ahead of them stands a mound of earth taller than any tree. On top of it sits the house of the city's leader. Little Fawn has climbed the steps of that mound only once, on a feast day.

The plaza is bigger than a whole village. It is packed with people. Some have walked in from farms a day away. Others came by canoe from far up the river. Little Fawn hears words she does not know. Traders from the south have brought seashells. Traders from the north have brought copper that shines like the sun. Her mother trades a basket of dried corn for a small copper bead.

In one corner of the plaza, men are playing chunkey. One player rolls a smooth stone disk across the ground. Two others throw long poles, trying to land closest to where the disk will stop. A crowd shouts and bets on the game. Little Fawn knows this game is played in villages hundreds of miles away. Cahokia's ideas travel as far as its traders do.

Near the edge of the city, Little Fawn passes a circle of tall wooden posts. A priest watches the sun through the posts to track the seasons. He will tell the farmers when to plant. Corn, beans and squash feed this city of thousands. Without them, there would be no plaza, no mound and no market.

Nobody in Little Fawn's world writes anything down. So how do we know about her city? Archaeologists dig into the soil and find house posts, broken pots, corn cobs, shell beads and copper. They measure the mounds. They count the houses. From those clues, they rebuild a day like this one. Cahokia's people left no books, but they left a city.
story.think: Cahokia had no writing. What kinds of things would you look for in the ground if you wanted to learn how its people lived?

lessons.title: The First People Arrive
lessons.mainIdea: People have lived in North America for at least fifteen thousand years, and we know it from the tools and bones they left behind.
reading: Long before any city, people walked and paddled into North America. Most scientists think they came from Asia. During the last *ice age*, so much water was frozen in ice that the sea was lower. Land connected Asia and Alaska. People may have crossed that land, or paddled along the coast. This happened at least fifteen thousand years ago. Some sites may be older.

How do we know? Nobody wrote it down. Instead, people left things behind. Near Clovis, New Mexico, hunters made long stone spear points. They dropped them next to the bones of mammoths. Scientists call these *artifacts*, objects that people made. They can tell how old an artifact is by testing the bone or charcoal found with it.

Illinois has these clues too. Farmers plowing fields have turned up stone spear points thousands of years old. Along the rivers, people fished and gathered nuts. Slowly they learned to grow plants. By about a thousand years ago, corn had become the main food in many places. That change made villages and cities possible.

words.d: a long time when much of Earth was covered by ice and the sea was lower
an object made or used by people long ago, such as a spear point or pot

look.title: A Spear Point in a Cornfield
look.text: A farmer in central Illinois picks up a gray stone from a plowed field. It is shaped like a leaf, with sharp edges and a groove at the base. A scientist says it is about ten thousand years old. No one has lived on that spot, as far as anyone knows, for a very long time.
look.prompt: What can this one stone tell us about the people who made it? What can it not tell us?

check.q: How long have people lived in North America?
check.why: The oldest sites are at least fifteen thousand years old, and some may be older.

check.q: Why could people walk from Asia to Alaska during the ice age?
choices: The sea was lower, so land was uncovered
The two places were always joined
check.why: So much water was frozen that the sea dropped, and land connected the two continents.

check.q: What is an artifact?
choices: An object made or used by people long ago
check.why: Artifacts are objects people made, like spear points and pots, and they are our main clues about people without writing.

lessons.title: Many Lands, Many Ways
lessons.mainIdea: Native peoples lived in hundreds of nations, each with its own language and its own way of living that fit its land.
reading: When Europeans arrived in the 1490s, millions of people already lived in North America. They did not belong to one group. They belonged to hundreds of *nations*. A nation is a people with its own land, its own leaders and its own language. The Lakota, the Hopi and the Haudenosaunee were as different from each other as Spain is from China.

The land shaped how each nation lived. In the forests of the east, people built homes from bark and grew corn. On the grassy plains, people hunted bison. In the dry Southwest, people built with mud brick and watered their crops by hand. On the rainy northwest coast, people fished for salmon and carved giant cedar trees. In the frozen north, people hunted seals on the ice.

Scientists call each of these areas a *culture region*. Nations in the same region often shared foods, homes and tools, because they faced the same weather and the same plants and animals. But they still had their own languages and stories. In this chapter you will visit five regions and one great city. Keep asking one question: how did the land shape the way people lived?

words.d: a people with its own land, leaders and language
a large area where peoples shared similar foods, homes and tools because of the land

look.title: Rain Across the Regions
look.unit: inches of rain or melted snow per year, rough
look.cite: Rounded typical figures for each region; National Weather Service averages
look.prompt: Which region would be easiest for growing corn? Which would be hardest? How might that change what people ate?

check.q: What is a nation?
choices: A people with its own land, leaders and language
check.why: Each Native nation had its own land, leaders and language, and there were hundreds of them.

check.q: Why did nations in the same region often share foods and homes?
choices: They faced the same weather, plants and animals
check.why: The same land gives the same materials and foods, so peoples in one region solved problems in similar ways.

check.q: Based on the rain data, where would farming be hardest?
check.why: The Arctic gets only about six inches of moisture a year and is frozen most of the year, so crops cannot grow there.

lessons.title: Longhouses of the Eastern Woodlands
lessons.mainIdea: In the eastern forests, people built longhouses from bark and grew corn, beans and squash together.
reading: Picture a forest of oak and maple that goes on for weeks of walking. This was the Eastern Woodlands, from the Atlantic coast to the Mississippi River. Wood was everywhere, so people built with it. The Haudenosaunee of what is now New York built *longhouses*. A longhouse had a frame of bent poles covered with sheets of elm bark. It could be as long as a school hallway.

Several related families lived in one longhouse. Each family had its own space along the wall, with a shared fire in the middle. The oldest woman in the family was in charge of the house. Other Woodlands peoples, like the Algonquian nations, built smaller round homes called wigwams. Both kinds of home used bark, because bark was free and easy to find.

Woodlands farmers planted three crops in the same mound of soil. They called them the *three sisters*: corn, beans and squash. The corn grew tall. The beans climbed the corn stalks. The squash spread its wide leaves on the ground and kept the soil damp. Beans also put back into the soil what corn used up. Together, the three sisters fed whole villages. Corn from these fields still shapes what Illinois grows today.

words.d: a long home with a pole frame and bark walls, shared by several related families
corn, beans and squash, planted together in one mound so each helps the others

look.title: Three Plants in One Mound
look.text: A Woodlands farmer pushes corn seeds into a small hill of soil. A few weeks later she plants beans beside the young corn. Then she plants squash around the edge. By late summer the corn is taller than she is, beans hang from the stalks, and huge squash leaves shade the ground so weeds cannot grow.
look.prompt: Why is planting the three crops together smarter than planting each in its own field?

check.q: What were longhouses made of?
choices: Bent poles and sheets of bark
check.why: The Woodlands were full of trees, so people built homes from poles and elm bark.

check.q: What did the beans do for the corn?
choices: They climbed the stalks and put good things back in the soil
check.why: Beans used the corn as a pole to climb, and they returned to the soil what the corn had used up.

check.q: Who was in charge of a Haudenosaunee longhouse?
choices: The chief of the whole nation
The oldest woman in the family
check.why: Longhouses belonged to the women of a family, and the oldest woman led the household.

lessons.title: Bison and Tipis on the Plains
lessons.mainIdea: On the treeless Great Plains, people depended on the bison for food, shelter, clothing and tools.
reading: West of the Mississippi the trees thin out. Then they stop. The Great Plains are a sea of grass that stretches from Texas to Canada. Millions of *bison*, the big shaggy animals many people call buffalo, grazed on that grass. Before Europeans came, there were tens of millions of them. For the peoples of the Plains, the bison was life.

Plains peoples used every part of the animal. Meat was eaten fresh or dried for winter. Hides became blankets, robes and the walls of homes. Bones became tools and needles. Horns became spoons. Even the stomach could be a cooking pot. Wasting a bison was unthinkable, because the whole village depended on it.

Bison herds moved with the seasons, so many Plains peoples moved too. Their home was the *tipi*, a cone of long poles covered with bison hides. A tipi could be taken down in minutes and packed onto a dog sled. Before Europeans brought horses, dogs did the hauling. Nations like the Lakota and Cheyenne followed the herds across the grass, and their homes came with them.

words.d: a large, shaggy grazing animal of the Plains, often called a buffalo
a cone-shaped home of poles and bison hides that could be moved quickly

look.title: Where the Bison Went
look.cite: Standard estimates used by the National Park Service and historians, rounded
look.prompt: What happened to the bison between 1870 and 1890? What would that have meant for people who depended on them?

check.q: Why did many Plains peoples move their homes during the year?
check.why: Bison moved with the seasons, and the people who depended on them moved too.

check.q: Before horses arrived, what carried a packed-up tipi?
check.why: Dogs pulled loads on small sleds until Europeans brought horses.

check.q: Which of these was NOT made from bison?
check.why: Bark canoes came from Woodlands trees. Hides made tipi walls, bones made needles, and horns made spoons.

lessons.title: Pueblos and Ditches of the Southwest
lessons.mainIdea: In the dry Southwest, people built towns of stone and mud brick and dug ditches to bring water to their corn.
reading: Now picture red cliffs, dry ground and a hot sun. This is the Southwest, in what is now Arizona and New Mexico. Rain is rare. Yet people have farmed here for more than two thousand years. The Ancestral Puebloans, the Hopi, the Zuni and others built towns of stone and mud brick. The Spanish later called these towns *pueblos*, their word for villages.

A pueblo looked like an apartment building made of earth. Rooms were stacked several stories high. People climbed ladders to reach the upper floors. Thick walls kept rooms cool in the day and warm at night. Some pueblos were built into the sides of cliffs, high above the valley floor. Others, like Acoma in New Mexico, sit on top of a mesa and have been lived in for hundreds of years.

Farming with so little rain took skill. People dug ditches to carry river water to their fields. This is called *irrigation*. They planted corn deep in the ground where the soil stayed damp. They saved seeds from the plants that survived dry years. Corn, beans and squash grew here too, along with cotton for clothes. The Hopi still plant corn in the desert today, using ways their families have kept for centuries.

words.d: a town of stone and mud brick with rooms stacked several stories high
bringing water to fields through ditches or canals

look.title: A Town in the Cliff
look.text: High on a cliff in southwest Colorado, stone rooms are tucked under a rock overhang. The rooms were built about eight hundred years ago. To get in, families climbed hand and toe holds cut into the cliff. From the doorways you can see the whole valley below.
look.prompt: Why might people choose to build their homes high in a cliff instead of down by the fields?

check.q: What is irrigation?
choices: Climbing a ladder to a roof
Saving seeds for the next year
Bringing water to fields through ditches
check.why: Southwest farmers dug ditches to carry river water to their crops because rain was rare.

check.q: Why did thick pueblo walls help people?
choices: They kept rooms cool by day and warm at night
check.why: Thick earth walls hold steady heat, which matters in a desert with hot days and cold nights.

check.q: Which peoples still live in pueblos in the Southwest today?
check.why: The Hopi, Zuni and other Pueblo peoples have lived in the Southwest for many centuries and still do.

lessons.title: Cedar and Salmon on the Northwest Coast
lessons.mainIdea: On the rainy Pacific Northwest coast, giant cedar trees and rivers full of salmon made rich villages possible.
reading: On the Pacific coast, from Oregon up to Alaska, it rains most of the year. Giant cedar trees grow taller than a ten-story building. Every spring and fall, rivers fill with *salmon* swimming upstream to lay their eggs. Peoples like the Haida, Tlingit and Chinook had so much food that they did not need to farm. They caught salmon by the thousands and dried and smoked them for winter.

Cedar was the wood for everything. People split the soft, straight-grained trunks into planks and built large houses. They hollowed whole logs into canoes that could go out on the ocean. They wove cedar bark into clothes, mats and baskets. And they carved tall cedar posts with animals and family symbols. These are the *totem poles* that stood in front of homes.

A totem pole is not a god or an idol. It is a family record. The carved raven, bear or whale shows the family's history and its rights. Rich families held a feast called a potlatch. The host gave away blankets, food and other gifts to hundreds of guests. Giving more away showed more honor. In this land of plenty, being generous was the way to become great.

words.d: a fish that swims from the ocean up rivers each year, the main food of the Northwest coast
a tall carved cedar post showing a family's animals, history and rights

look.title: The Day the River Turned Silver
look.text: In late summer a Chinook boy stands on a wooden platform over a rushing river. Below him the water is so thick with salmon that it flashes silver. His uncle dips a net and lifts out three fish at once. By nightfall the drying racks are full. There will be food all winter without planting a single seed.
look.prompt: Why did people here have time to carve, build and hold big feasts when Plains peoples had to keep moving?

check.q: Why did Northwest coast peoples not need to farm?
choices: Rivers full of salmon gave them plenty of food
They traded with the Plains for food
It was too cold for plants
check.why: The salmon runs gave so much food that people could dry and store enough for the whole year.

check.q: What does a totem pole show?
choices: A family's animals, history and rights
check.why: The carved animals are family symbols that tell the family's story and what it is entitled to.

check.q: At a potlatch, how did a host show honor?
check.why: Giving wealth away to guests was the way a family earned respect on the Northwest coast.

lessons.title: Ice and Sea in the Arctic
lessons.mainIdea: In the Arctic, where nothing can be farmed, the Inuit lived by hunting seals and whales and inventing tools for ice and sea.
reading: At the top of the continent, the ground stays frozen all year. No trees grow. In winter the sun barely rises. This is the Arctic, home of the Inuit and their relatives across Alaska, Canada and Greenland. You cannot farm here. But the sea is full of life. Seals, walrus, whales and fish became food, fuel and clothing.

Inuit inventions fit this world exactly. The *kayak* was a light one-person boat with a skin cover stretched over a frame. A hunter sat inside, sealed against the icy water. Sleds pulled by dogs crossed the snow. Boots and parkas were sewn from seal and caribou skins with sinew thread. Seal oil burned in stone lamps for light and heat.

In winter some Inuit families built domed houses from blocks of packed snow. The snow held in body heat. In summer they lived in tents of skin. They knew the ice the way a farmer knows a field: which ice would hold, which would break, where seals came up to breathe. Today Inuit still hunt in the Arctic, often by snowmobile, and their languages are still spoken.

words.d: the far north around the North Pole, where the ground stays frozen and no trees grow
a light, covered one-person boat with a skin cover over a frame

look.title: Waiting at the Breathing Hole
look.text: An Inuit hunter stands still on the sea ice with a spear. In front of him is a small hole in the ice. Under the ice, a seal must come up to breathe every few minutes. It might use this hole. The hunter has waited two hours. His parka is seal skin. His boots are caribou. His spear tip is walrus tusk.
look.prompt: Count the animals this hunter depends on just to stand there. What would happen to his family if the seals disappeared?

check.q: Why could Inuit not farm?
choices: The ground stays frozen all year
check.why: Frozen ground and a dark, cold winter make farming impossible in the Arctic.

check.q: What is a kayak?
choices: A light covered boat for one person
check.why: The kayak was a skin-covered boat that let a hunter go out on icy water without getting wet.

check.q: Why did a snow house stay warm inside?
choices: A big wood fire burned inside
The sun shone through the walls
Packed snow held in the people's body heat
The walls were made of seal skin
check.why: Snow traps air, so a snow dome holds in warmth from bodies and a small oil lamp. There was no wood to burn.

lessons.title: Cahokia, a City of Mounds
lessons.mainIdea: Around the year 1100, Cahokia in Illinois was the largest city north of Mexico, built by farmers who raised huge mounds of earth.
reading: Cahokia stood on the east side of the Mississippi River, across from what is now St. Louis. It was in Illinois. Around the year 1100 it may have held ten thousand to twenty thousand people. No city in the United States would be that big again until Philadelphia in the 1700s. Its people belonged to a way of life scientists call Mississippian.

The city was famous for its *mounds*. People carried soil in baskets, one load at a time, and piled it up. The biggest, now called Monks Mound, is about one hundred feet tall. Its base covers about fourteen acres, more than ten football fields. About one hundred twenty mounds once stood in the city. Leaders lived on top of some. Others held the dead.

Corn made Cahokia possible. Farmers in the rich river bottom grew enough to feed thousands of people who did not farm: builders, priests, potters, traders. By about 1350, the city was empty. Nobody knows exactly why. Floods, crop failures, war and worn-out soil are all possible. The mounds still stand at Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site, and you can climb Monks Mound today.

words.d: a hill made by people piling up earth, basket by basket
the way of life of the corn-farming, mound-building peoples of the Mississippi valley around 800 to 1500

look.title: Cahokia by the Numbers
rows: Base of Monks Mound in acres
People at its peak, low estimate
People at its peak, high estimate
look.unit: feet, acres, mounds or people, rounded
look.cite: Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site; standard estimates, rounded
look.prompt: Every basket of dirt in Monks Mound was carried by a person. What does that tell you about how Cahokia's people were organized?

check.q: Where was Cahokia?
choices: In Illinois, across the river from St. Louis
check.why: Cahokia stood in the Mississippi river bottom in southern Illinois.

check.q: How were the mounds built?
choices: People carried soil in baskets and piled it up
check.why: There were no horses or wheels. People carried the earth one basket at a time.

check.q: What made it possible for a city of thousands to exist?
choices: Corn farming in the rich river soil
check.why: Corn from the river bottom fed the many people who built, traded and led instead of farming.

lessons.title: The Haudenosaunee Council
lessons.mainIdea: Five nations in the Northeast joined under the Great Law of Peace, with a council that decided together and clan mothers who chose the leaders.
reading: Long before the United States, five nations in what is now New York State were at war with each other. According to their own history, a man called the Peacemaker traveled among them. He urged them to stop fighting and join together. The Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca agreed. They called themselves the Haudenosaunee, the people of the longhouse. Later the Tuscarora joined as a sixth nation.

Their agreement is called the Great Law of Peace. It set up a *confederacy*, a group of nations that stay separate but act together on big matters. Each nation sent chiefs to a Grand Council. The council met at Onondaga, in the middle. Chiefs talked until they agreed. No one nation could force the others. A war against one was a war against all.

Women held real power. Each family belonged to a clan, and the oldest women, the *clan mothers*, chose the chiefs. If a chief did wrong, a clan mother could remove him. Some early Americans, including Benjamin Franklin, knew about the council and admired how the nations worked together. The Haudenosaunee Grand Council still meets today.

words.d: a group of nations that stay separate but join together to act on big decisions
the senior woman of a clan, who chose and could remove chiefs

look.title: Words of the Great Law
look.text: The Great Law of Peace, passed down by speech and wampum, says that the chiefs of the council must have skin seven spans thick, so that anger and hard words do not pierce them. It tells leaders to think not of themselves, but of the people to come, even the children not yet born.
look.cite: Haudenosaunee Great Law of Peace, oral tradition first written down in the 1800s (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What does it mean for a leader to have skin seven spans thick? Why would a council want leaders like that?

check.q: What did the Great Law of Peace do?
choices: Made one nation rule the others
Joined five nations in a confederacy that decided together
check.why: The five nations stayed separate but agreed to act together and stop fighting each other.

check.q: Who chose the chiefs?
check.why: The senior women of each clan chose the chiefs and could remove them.

check.q: Which nation joined the confederacy later as the sixth?
check.why: The original five were Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca. The Tuscarora joined in the 1700s.

lessons.title: Stories, Art and Trade Routes
lessons.mainIdea: Native peoples passed down knowledge through spoken stories and art, and traded goods across thousands of miles.
reading: Most Native nations did not use writing. Instead, they kept their history by *oral tradition*, passing stories from one generation to the next by speech. Elders told how the world began, how the clan got its name and where the boundaries were. Children heard the stories many times until they knew them. A good storyteller was as important as a good hunter.

Art carried memory too. The Haudenosaunee wove beads of white and purple shell into belts called *wampum*. A wampum belt recorded a treaty or an important event. Its pattern was read aloud at council. Plains peoples painted the year's big event on a bison hide, adding one picture each winter. Pueblo potters painted designs that told who made the pot and where.

Trade tied the continent together. Archaeologists at Cahokia have found copper from Lake Superior, seashells from the Gulf of Mexico and a shiny stone from the Rocky Mountains. Each of these traveled hundreds of miles by canoe and on foot. Goods, ideas and games moved along the same paths. When Europeans arrived, they walked onto trails that were already old.

words.d: history and knowledge kept by telling it aloud from one generation to the next
belts of white and purple shell beads used to record treaties and events

look.title: An Early Visitor Sees the Mounds
look.text: In 1811 an American traveler named Henry Brackenridge walked among the mounds at Cahokia. He wrote that when he came to the great mound, he was struck with astonishment. He said that a city of thousands must have stood there, and that raising such a work must have taken years of labor by many people.
look.cite: Henry Brackenridge, letter and travel writing, 1811 to 1814 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Brackenridge saw the mounds but not the people. What clues did he use to guess that a large city had stood there?

check.q: What is oral tradition?
check.why: Without writing, people kept their history by telling it aloud and having the young learn it.

check.q: What does copper from Lake Superior found at Cahokia prove?
choices: Cahokia's people were from the north
Trade goods traveled hundreds of miles
check.why: Lake Superior is far from Cahokia, so the copper had to be carried there by trade.

check.q: What was a wampum belt used for?
choices: Recording a treaty or important event
check.why: The bead patterns recorded agreements and were read aloud at council meetings.

lessons.title: Native Nations Today
lessons.mainIdea: Native nations are still here: more than five hundred are recognized by the United States, and tens of thousands of Native people live in Illinois, many in Chicago.
reading: Native peoples are not only part of the past. Today the United States recognizes more than five hundred seventy Native nations. Each is a *sovereign* nation, which means it has its own government, laws and leaders. Many have their own lands, called reservations. Others do not. Their citizens are also citizens of the United States.

Illinois is named for the Illinois people, who called themselves the Illiniwek. Most of their descendants were pushed west in the 1800s and now belong to the Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma. The Potawatomi, Kickapoo, Miami, Sauk, Meskwaki and Ho-Chunk also lived here. In recent years the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation regained some of its land in northern Illinois.

Chicago today has one of the largest urban Native populations in the country. Native people from many nations moved there for work in the 1900s. The American Indian Center of Chicago, founded in 1953, holds a powwow every year. Native students go to Chicago schools. Native artists, doctors and lawyers work across the state. The first peoples are still here, still speaking, still building.

words.d: having the right to govern itself with its own laws and leaders
land that belongs to a Native nation and is governed by it
a gathering with dancing, drumming and singing where Native people from many nations meet

look.title: A Powwow on the North Side
look.text: On a fall weekend in Chicago, a drum sounds in a park. Dancers in beaded and feathered outfits move in a circle. One dancer is Lakota. Another is Ojibwe. Another is Navajo. A grandmother sells fry bread. A teenager checks her phone between dances. A city bus rolls by on the street.
look.prompt: What in this scene is old, and what is new? Why is it a mistake to think of Native people only as part of the past?

check.q: What does it mean that a Native nation is sovereign?
choices: It is part of the past
It has its own government and laws
check.why: Sovereign means self-governing. Recognized Native nations run their own governments.

check.q: Where do most descendants of the Illinois people live today?
check.why: The Illinois were pushed west in the 1800s, and their descendants are the Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma.

check.q: About how many Native nations does the United States recognize today?
check.why: There are more than five hundred seventy federally recognized nations, each with its own government.

review.q: What is the main way we know about people who lived here before writing?
choices: Artifacts like spear points and pots found in the ground
review.why: Artifacts, mounds and bones are the evidence scientists use to learn about people who did not write.

review.q: Which region's peoples lived mainly by hunting bison?
review.why: Tens of millions of bison lived on the Plains, and Plains peoples used every part of them.

review.q: Why did Southwest peoples use irrigation?
choices: To water crops in a land with little rain
review.why: Rain is rare in the Southwest, so farmers dug ditches to bring river water to their corn.

review.q: Which best explains why homes differed from region to region?
choices: One leader chose each home style
All peoples used the same wood
People built with what their land provided
review.why: Bark in the forests, hides on the Plains, mud brick in the desert, cedar on the coast, snow in the Arctic.

review.q: Which of these was true of Cahokia around the year 1100?
choices: It was the largest city north of Mexico
It was built by the Spanish
It was on the Pacific coast
review.why: Cahokia held ten to twenty thousand people fed by corn farming in the Mississippi valley.

review.q: How did the Haudenosaunee Grand Council make decisions?
choices: Chiefs from each nation talked until they agreed
review.why: No nation could force the others. The chiefs discussed until they reached agreement.

review.q: Seashells from the Gulf of Mexico were found at Cahokia. What does this show?
choices: The shells were dropped by birds
Trade routes reached hundreds of miles
review.why: The Gulf is far south of Illinois, so the shells reached Cahokia by long-distance trade.

review.q: Which statement about Native people today is correct?
choices: They no longer exist as nations
They live only in the West
More than five hundred seventy nations are recognized, and many Native people live in cities like Chicago
review.why: Native nations are sovereign today, and Chicago has one of the largest urban Native populations.
